core: What the person-in-environment perspective claims: difficulty is read in the transaction between a person and the settings they live in
Perspective versus theory: PIE directs attention and generates questions; it does not predict outcomes
Intellectual roots: Richmond's social diagnosis, the settlement house tradition, the systems and ecological turn, Germain and Gitterman's Life Model
Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems model as an adjacent influence, with its micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono levels and its later bioecological revision
Ecomap and genogram: what each actually shows and what neither does
Social determinants of health (Healthy People 2030) as the contemporary evidence-based expression of the same idea
The practical payoff: a person-in-environment reading changes which interventions look plausible
Two boundaries: PIE is not environmental determinism, and the PIE System classification is not the general perspective
supporting: Micro, mezzo and macro levels as a way of sorting environmental information
The role of the client's own perception of their situation
The narrowing of 'environment' to the social environment in standard usage
outOfScope: Strengths-based practice as a practice model (separate topic)
Poverty measurement and social inequality (separate topic)
Social work roles, settings, licensure and job titles (owned by the parallel 'what social workers and human-service professionals do' topic)
Any individualized clinical, diagnostic, treatment, legal or benefits-eligibility guidance

claims.claim: U.S. social work accreditation standards define the profession's purpose and generalist practice as guided by and grounded in a person-in-environment framework, and pair 'person-in-environment' with theories of human behavior across the engagement, assessment, intervention and evaluation competencies.
Person-in-environment functions as an orienting perspective or framework that directs where a practitioner looks, not as a theory that generates testable predictions about outcomes.

Mary Richmond's Social Diagnosis (1917) defined social diagnosis as defining as exactly as possible the situation and personality of a person in social need in relation to the people they depend on or who depend on them and in relation to the social institutions of their community, placing community institutions inside the profession's first systematic casework method.

Hull-House, established in Chicago in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr, was the first settlement house in the United States and combined direct services with neighbourhood and structural reform such as protective labour laws and housing and sanitation work.

Germain and Gitterman's Life Model, first published in 1980 and now in a fourth edition with Carolyn Knight (2021), brought the ecological perspective into social work practice method, organising work around life stressors and person-environment fit and aiming interventions at communities, organisations and policymakers as well as at individuals.

Bronfenbrenner's 1979 monograph named the microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem and macrosystem; the chronosystem was introduced in his later work; and he subsequently reworked the framework into the Process-Person-Context-Time (bioecological) model in which proximal processes are central.

Reviews of applied research find that studies which stop at Bronfenbrenner's nested contextual circles and neglect proximal processes misrepresent the theory, which is the developmental-psychology form of the same error as reading person-in-environment as pure environmental determinism.

An ecomap diagrams an individual's or household's current social and personal connections to outside systems and the quality of those connections; it is credited to social worker Ann Hartman in the mid-1970s.

Federal child welfare practice guidance instructs caseworkers to build an ecomap and a genogram with parents to record family history and the current extended family and support system, and to add to both after meeting children and reviewing records, providers and the wider support system.

Healthy People 2030 defines social determinants of health as the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship and age that affect health, functioning and quality-of-life outcomes and risks, and groups them into five domains: Economic Stability; Education Access and Quality; Health Care Access and Quality; Neighborhood and Built Environment; and Social and Community Context.

Healthy People 2030 states that promoting healthy choices alone will not eliminate health disparities and directs attention to upstream conditions usually unrelated to health care delivery, which is a population-level statement about distributions rather than a prediction about any individual.

The PIE System is a distinct four-factor classification (Factor I social role and relationship functioning problems; Factor II environmental problems across six system types; Factor III mental health; Factor IV physical health) published by NASW Press, in which Factors I and II form the core social work description while Factors III and IV borrow other professions' classifications.

The PIE System manual states explicitly that PIE is not an interview guide and includes a strengths component alongside each factor, which confirms the classification is a recording and description instrument rather than an explanatory theory or an assessment protocol.
In mainstream social work usage the 'environment' of person-in-environment has repeatedly narrowed to the social environment, with the physical and built environment dropping out without explanation.

Ecological theory as taught in social work holds that how a person perceives and interprets their environment shapes their functioning, so the perspective retains the person's own interpretation rather than treating the person as an object acted on by surroundings.

positions: Several open social work and human services texts state that Ann Hartman, who developed the ecomap, is also credited with developing the genogram.
The family therapy literature credits Murray Bowen's 'family diagram' and the standardised notation published by Monica McGoldrick and Randy Gerson in 1985.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No authoritative source was found that settles the attribution, so the lesson does not name an originator for the genogram. It describes only what a genogram shows, which federal practice guidance and the open texts agree on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The date of the ecomap's introduction.
positions: Open textbooks state the eco-map was developed in 1975 by Ann Hartman.
The journal record for Hartman's 'Diagrammatic Assessment of Family Relationships' in Social Casework is indexed as 1978.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says 'the mid-1970s' and credits Hartman, which both positions support, rather than fixing a year the sources disagree about.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'environment' in person-in-environment includes the physical and natural world.
positions: The perspective as stated is about the whole environment a person inhabits.
Zapf documents that in mainstream social work usage the environment repeatedly becomes the social environment, with the physical environment dropping out unremarked.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the broad version and names the narrowing explicitly as a known limitation of ordinary usage, attributed as a critique rather than as settled fact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Bronfenbrenner's model should be presented as five nested levels.
positions: Social work and human services texts teach five levels including the chronosystem.

A peer-reviewed review notes the chronosystem postdates the 1979 monograph and that Bronfenbrenner later reworked the framework into the Process-Person-Context-Time model, in which stopping at the nested circles misrepresents the theory.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the five levels because that is how social work courses use them, and states in the same breath that the levels are a borrowing from developmental psychology and that Bronfenbrenner himself moved past a purely contextual reading.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing specific about person-in-environment at all; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('a concept students use to organize information') that no source supports as a description of this perspective.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined the term as 'a foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and carries no content.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'reading a map legend') described studying vocabulary rather than the concept, and had no statement of where the analogy fails.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested generic study habits rather than any person-in-environment content, and offered three options each rather than four.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson body with sourced content on the perspective's claim, roots, tools, contemporary evidence base and practical consequences.
Added the precision that person-in-environment is a perspective or framework rather than a theory that predicts outcomes, which the draft never raised.
Added the environmental-determinism correction and the statement that the perspective does not deny agency or biology.
Separated the PIE System classification (Karls and Wandrei 1994; Karls and O'Keefe 2008) from the general perspective, since the shared acronym is a standing source of student confusion.
Grounded the contemporary evidence in the Healthy People 2030 social determinants of health framing, including its five domains and its explicit population-level scope.
Distinguished what an ecomap shows from what a genogram shows, and stated that neither instrument measures anything.
Referenced but did not teach strengths-based practice, trauma-informed care, poverty, cultural humility and needs-assessment procedure, which are separate topics in this subject.
rightsIssues: The NASW Press PIE manual is copyrighted; only its factual structure was used and no wording was reproduced.
CSWE's 2022 EPAS is copyrighted; its person-in-environment language was read and described in original wording, not quoted at length.
Zapf (2010) is CC BY-NC-ND, which forbids derivatives, so it was used strictly as a reference for facts and framing.
Tyler's Human Behavior and the Social Environment I is CC BY-NC-SA, which is incompatible with reuse in this project, so it was used only to confirm how the concept is conventionally taught.
Richmond's Social Diagnosis (1917) is in the US public domain; even so, no extended excerpt is stored or reproduced.
No source was paraphrase-followed. All lesson prose is original.

sourceRecords.title: 2022 Educational Policy and Accreditation Standards for Baccalaureate and Master's Social Work Programs
sourceRecords.notes: Accreditation standard. Verified by extracting the PDF text: the profession's purpose is 'Guided by a person-in-environment framework'; 'Generalist practice is grounded in the liberal arts and the person-in-environment framework'; Competencies 6, 7, 8 and 9 each pair 'theories of human behavior and person-in-environment' with interprofessional conceptual frameworks. Used to support that PIE is treated as a framework/perspective rather than a predictive theory, and that it is curricular bedrock. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social Determinants of Health - Healthy People 2030
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
sourceRecords.notes: Federal health objectives. Verified directly: SDOH defined as the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship and age that affect health, functioning and quality-of-life outcomes and risks; grouped into five domains (Economic Stability; Education Access and Quality; Health Care Access and Quality; Neighborhood and Built Environment; Social and Community Context); one of five overarching goals targets social, physical and economic environments; page states plainly that promoting healthy choices alone will not eliminate disparities and emphasises 'upstream' factors usually unrelated to health care delivery. Facts synthesised; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Person-in-Environment System Manual, 2nd Edition (sample chapters: Structure of the PIE System; How to Use PIE in Practice)
sourceRecords.provider: NASW Press - James M. Karls and Maura E. O'Keefe
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher-posted sample chapters of the PIE System manual (2nd ed., NASW Press, 2008, ISBN 978-0-87101-379-8; publisher page https://naswpress.org/product/person-in-environment-system-manual/ confirms authors, edition and year, and describes PIE as an alternative to disease and moral models). Text extracted and read. Confirms the four factors (I Social Functioning / Social Role and Relationship Problems; II Environmental Problems; III Mental Health; IV Physical Health), that Factors I and II are the core social work description while III and IV borrow other professions' classifications, the six Factor II system types, the strengths component, and the manual's explicit statement that PIE is not an interview guide. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social Diagnosis
sourceRecords.provider: Mary E. Richmond, Russell Sage Foundation (1917), via Internet Archive
sourceRecords.notes: Primary historical source, published 1917 and therefore in the US public domain. Full OCR text read. Richmond's own chapter summary defines social diagnosis as the attempt to define as exactly as possible the situation and personality of a person in social need in relation to the other human beings on whom they depend or who depend on them, and in relation to the social institutions of their community. Used to ground the claim that the profession's first systematic method already placed community institutions inside the unit of study. Facts synthesised; no extended excerpt stored or reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Hull-House
sourceRecords.provider: National Park Service, U.S. Department of the Interior
sourceRecords.notes: Federal historical reference. Confirms Hull-House was established in Chicago in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr as the first settlement house in the United States, that it provided direct services (legal aid, employment office, childcare, training), and that residents pursued neighbourhood and structural reform including protective labour laws and housing and sanitation problems. Used for the settlement-house half of PIE's intellectual inheritance.

sourceRecords.title: Review of studies applying Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory in international and intercultural education research
sourceRecords.provider: Peiru Tong and I-Shin An, Frontiers in Psychology 14:1233925 (2024)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed open-access review (licence confirmed on the article page). Supports: the 1979 monograph named microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem and macrosystem; the chronosystem came from Bronfenbrenner's later work rather than the original monograph; he subsequently reworked the framework into the Process-Person-Context-Time (bioecological) model; and reviews find that applications which stop at the nested contextual circles and neglect proximal processes misrepresent the theory. Facts synthesised; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Social Work and the Environment: Understanding People and Place
sourceRecords.provider: Michael Kim Zapf, Critical Social Work 11(3) (2010)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed open-access critique (journal states CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no-derivatives, so treated as reference only). Full text read. Supports: person-in-environment is described as the profession's conventional metaphor/perspective rather than a predictive theory, and the 'environment' in mainstream social work usage repeatedly collapses into the social environment with the physical and built environment dropping out unremarked. Used for the precision points about what PIE is and what its standard reading leaves out.

sourceRecords.title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment I - The Person in Environment
sourceRecords.provider: Susan Tyler, University of Arkansas Pressbooks (2020)
sourceRecords.notes: Open social work text (licence shown on the page). Read in full. Corroborates the standard undergraduate treatment: person-in-environment as an orienting approach, micro/mezzo/macro levels, systems theory, ecological theory including the role of the client's own perception of their situation, and Bronfenbrenner's five levels. NC-SA terms are incompatible with reuse here, so it was used only to check that this lesson matches how the concept is actually taught; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Comprehensive Family Assessment Guidelines for Child Welfare
sourceRecords.provider: Children's Bureau, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2005)
sourceRecords.notes: Federal practice guidance. PDF text extracted and searched: the guidelines direct caseworkers to use the ecomap and genogram with parents to record family history and the current extended family and support system, and to add to both after meeting children and reviewing records, providers and the extended support system. Used to show these are working instruments in federally guided practice, not classroom exercises.

sourceRecords.title: Generalist Practice - Introduction to Human Services
sourceRecords.provider: Open Oregon Educational Resources (chapter by Aikia Fricke and Ferris State University Department of Social Work)
sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook chapter (attribution statement on the page licenses the chapter CC BY 4.0). Read in full. Supports the standard descriptions of the eco-map as a diagram of an individual's social and personal relationships with their environment, credited to Ann Hartman in the mid-1970s, and of Bronfenbrenner's five levels as they are taught in human services. No prose adapted; used to verify the conventional teaching.

sourceRecords.title: The Life Model of Social Work Practice: Advances in Theory and Practice, Fourth Edition
sourceRecords.provider: Columbia University Press - Alex Gitterman, Carolyn Knight and Carel B. Germain (2021)
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher record for the current edition. Confirms the Life Model introduced the ecological perspective into social work practice (first published 1980 by Germain and Gitterman), that it works at the people-environment interface, that it organises practice around life stressors including stressful life transitions, traumatic events and environmental stressors, and that it aims simultaneously at helping people and at influencing communities, organisations and policymakers. Used for attribution and framing only.
